summary: The ASA 2008 machine checkout is a genuinely safety-relevant daily ritual, not a box-ticking formality — completing it is directly associated with reduced anesthetic morbidity and mortality, and the whole point is catching equipment failure before it ever reaches a patient.
whyThisMatters: This module addresses a different 'pre-' checklist than the patient-facing preanesthesia-checklist — that one covers the patient (fasting, allergies, consent), this one covers the machine itself, and conflating the two risks skipping the equipment check because 'the pre-anesthesia checklist was already done.'
clinicalTakeaway:
Perform a FULL checkout at the start of each day, or whenever the machine is moved, serviced, or a vaporizer is changed — roughly 15 items, taking under 5 minutes.

An ABBREVIATED between-case check (roughly 8 of those items) is done before each subsequent case that day.

Priority items:
- Confirm backup ventilation equipment (a self-inflating bag connected to an oxygen source) is present and functional — know exactly where it is and that it works BEFORE an emergency, not during one.
- Leak-test the breathing circuit under positive pressure — a slow leak can silently under-deliver ventilation for an entire case without an obvious alarm.

This is genuinely associated with reduced anesthetic morbidity/mortality in the literature — treat it as a real safety check, not a formality to rush through.

body.text: Full checkout — start of day, or after moving/servicing/vaporizer change

The 2008 ASA recommendations specify roughly 15 items to check/verify at the start of each day, or whenever the machine is moved, serviced, or a vaporizer is changed. This typically takes under 5 minutes. Core components:

items: BACKUP VENTILATION — verify a self-inflating resuscitation bag and an alternate oxygen source are present and functional. This is item one for a reason: know exactly where it is and that it actually works before you're reaching for it during a machine failure, not discovering a problem with it in that moment.
GAS SUPPLY — check pipeline gas pressures (oxygen, air, nitrous if applicable) and verify backup cylinder gas supply/pressure in case of pipeline failure.
GAS FLOW AND LEAK TESTING — verify flow control function and perform a LOW-PRESSURE LEAK TEST of the machine's internal gas delivery system.
VAPORIZERS — confirm adequate fill level and secure mounting/locking of volatile agent vaporizers.

BREATHING CIRCUIT — leak-test the circuit itself under POSITIVE PRESSURE (a separate test from the low-pressure system leak test above) — this specifically catches a leak in the patient-facing circuit that could silently under-deliver ventilation during the case without triggering an obvious alarm.
SCAVENGING SYSTEM — verify proper function to ensure waste anesthetic gas is being appropriately removed from the OR environment.
VENTILATOR — verify functional operation, including alarm function.
MONITORS — confirm all monitoring systems are calibrated and operational before the first case.

body.text: A shorter subset (roughly 8 of the full 15 items) is performed before each subsequent case on a day when the full checkout has already been completed — this typically takes under 2 minutes and focuses on the items most relevant to verify fresh for each new patient/case setup (circuit integrity, gas flow, backup ventilation availability) rather than re-verifying every item from the full checkout.

This is distinct from the preanesthesia-checklist module, which covers the PATIENT-facing preoperative review (fasting status, allergies, consent, relevant history) — both share the word 'pre-' in their names but address entirely different safety domains. Completing one is not a substitute for the other.

Completion of a structured anesthesia equipment checkout procedure is associated with a measurable reduction in anesthetic morbidity and mortality in the literature — this isn't a box-ticking ritual performed out of habit or regulatory requirement alone.

Equipment failure (a leaking circuit, an empty backup oxygen cylinder, a malfunctioning vaporizer) caught during this checkout is equipment failure that never has the chance to affect an actual patient. The entire value of the checkout is front-loading that discovery to a moment with no patient yet connected, rather than discovering it mid-case.
